#1274. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

Chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Caicedo rattles the woodwork with a stunning effort! 💥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/CSIM9ogtSp

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

He told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

"Not as good as we wanted." 💬 David Moyes reflects on Everton's defeat to Chelsea 🔵 🎙️ @jules_breach | Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/qPU64VjHYC

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Xabi Alonso gives relatively positive news on Emi Martinez.

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and says, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

On his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that says when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”

With Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really important. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”

You can follow all the 3pm games here with our clockwatch.

Leading the charge for your attention is Brentford, who welcome Liverpool.

In a quick post-match interview with TNT Sports, Chelsea forward Pedro Neto says “this win is for him” after Martinez’s grim injury.

He said: “A shame for Emi but we wish him all the best … this win is for him. A clean sheet in his honour. In the second half we adjusted some stuff.”

Xabi Alonso leads the celebrations as Chelsea salute the away end! 🥳 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/AfwQAdYAmu

Everton are now in sixth place, but they might drop further. Their are five teams beneath them who would leapfrog them with a win, and Liverpool, Hull and Leeds amongst them are just a point behind.

Three points for Chelsea, who move into fourth place and keep their first Premier League clean sheet in nine months. Everton were enthusiastic, but they were ragged and then fell away once they went behind.

Chelsea, meanwhile, started loosely but tightened up, and became increasingly efficient.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1273. Everton In The Community's Vital Work Highlighted In £80.1m Social Value Report

Everton in the Community (EitC) supported more than 46,400 people through its programmes during the 2025/26 season – an increase of almost 10,000 on the previous year – according to the charity's latest Impact Report, which also highlights its £80.1 million annual social value.

Dedicated to breaking down barriers and tackling social inequality since 1988, the charitable arm of Everton Football Club supports some of the most vulnerable and underrepresented members of its local community.

Through more than 50 evidence-based, inclusive programmes, EitC addresses health inequalities, creates pathways into education and employment, and tackles crime and anti-social behaviour. Its work continues to evolve in response to local needs.

During the 2025/26 season alone, Everton in the Community supported 46,463 people while more than 156,000 individuals were reached through wider community engagement activity.

As Everton Football Club moved to Hill Dickinson Stadium at the start of the season, EitC made a conscious decision to remain rooted in L4, protecting Goodison Park's community legacy while continuing to invest in one of England's most deprived neighbourhoods.  

The charity’s mission continued to be shaped by the Trinity Project, its five-year strategy to ‘create stronger communities and brighter futures’ for all through three key pillars designed to drive lasting change: Minds, Learns and Thrives. 

Speaking about the latest Impact Report, Chief Executive Officer of Everton in the Community, Sue Gregory said: “Every year, this report provides an opportunity to reflect on what we have achieved together, and once again, I am incredibly proud of the difference our charity has made to tens of thousands of lives across Liverpool City Region.

“At Everton in the Community, we believe football has the power to do far more than just entertain. It has the ability to inspire, connect people, tackle inequality and create lasting change.”

More than half of children in Liverpool live in income-deprived families, compared with 38% nationally, while the cost-of-living crisis continues to place increasing pressure on local households and contribute to food insecurity.

Everton in the Community supported 1,293 people experiencing poverty, providing access to food, housing and debt advice, alongside high-quality, discounted food through its weekly Blue Base Pantry.

Health inequalities remain a significant challenge across Liverpool City Region, with local communities experiencing some of the poorest health outcomes and highest levels of poor mental health in the country. 

EitC is working to address these inequalities by bringing vital healthcare services directly into trusted community settings, helping people access support and identify health concerns earlier.

One example highlighted in the latest Impact Report is the award-winning BEAT Breathlessness Hub, which last season alone provided more than 900 people with access to heart and lung screenings and helped reduce the clinical pathway for heart failure from six months to one hour.

Mental health support also remained a key priority, with EitC supporting more than 9,000 people across the Liverpool City Region during the season and engaging 1,215 supporters through its ‘Together Against Suicide’ matchday support service.

The charity also helped tackle social isolation by providing weekly social activities for 217 older residents and supported people living with dementia and their carers through its ‘Pass on the Memories’ programme.

Educational inequality remains a significant challenge across Merseyside. Seven of the 20 constituencies in the country with the highest levels of special educational needs among children are in the region, with Liverpool Walton recording the highest percentage nationally. In parts of North Liverpool, almost a third of the working-age population also have no formal qualifications.

EitC works to remove barriers and widen pathways into education, training and employment for people of all ages – supporting children from their earliest years through to young people and adults preparing for future careers.

During the 2025/26 season, 16,583 people were supported on their educational journey, including 488 children who were helped to achieve their Early Learning Goals.

The charity also supported more than 2,500 young people identified as being at risk of becoming NEET, while helping 90 people move into employment and 13 into apprenticeships.

Speaking about the future, Sue continued: “We know that the landscape around us continues to change. 

“Financial pressures, inequality, poverty, poor mental health and barriers to education and employment are placing increasing demands on communities and the organisations supporting them. This makes our role more important than ever.

“None of this would be possible without our incredible staff, volunteers, participants, partners, donors and supporters. Together, we have built something truly special.

“The next chapter is only just the beginning, and I am incredibly excited about what we can achieve together.”

To read the latest Impact Report in full, click here. For more information about Everton in the Community’s 50+ programmes, visit our website here.

#1272. Tarkowski On Individual Form & Hopes For Everton Response

James Tarkowski has commended Everton’s ability to bounce back from defeat as his side look to rediscover their strong form following Saturday’s 2-0 loss against Chelsea.

That result marked the end to Everton’s undefeated start to the campaign, and the Blues face a tough text next, travelling to north London to take on reigning Premier League champions Arsenal.

Tarkowski told evertontv: “I always felt last year that anytime we suffered a defeat, we responded pretty well. So, hopefully that happens [this weekend].

“Hopefully, the team can keep picking up points. [Chelsea] was a tough day, a setback.

“We dealt with them pretty well last year, so we’re looking forward to [the next match].”

The Toffees skipper has enjoyed a strong season so far, often putting in standout showings from the Blues backline.

He tops the Premier League for successful duels (57) while ranking second in the division for interceptions (22).

Discussing his positive performances this term, Tarkowski added: “I feel good, I feel fit, I feel strong.

“It’s been nice to have a full pre-season behind me to build into the season. The team’s in a good place, I’m feeling good.

“I just want to continue playing week in and week out – that’s the most-important thing for me.”

#1271. My Everton #176: Toffee Lady Passes Late Fitness Test

Although I was born and raised near Manchester, my dad, aunt and grandad were all fanatical Toffees and made sure that my younger sister, Ceri, and I followed the correct path of football allegiance.

Dad enrolled us both in the junior Evertonian scheme, which gave us a small chance of having our names drawn out of the hat to be the matchday Toffee Lady mascot at Goodison Park.

One Thursday in December 2008, when I was six, my dad took a call from someone at Everton. The Toffee Lady for that Sunday’s televised match against Aston Villa had been taken ill, so my name had been the next to be drawn out.

Dad couldn’t wait to share the exciting news with us all. The only problem was that I had gone down with a heavy cold – but there was no way I was going to fail a late fitness test.

After a dose of Calpol I arrived at Goodison with my dad, grandad and aunt. I was wearing my dad’s old late 1970s Everton home shirt, which impressed Duncan McKenzie as he passed through the foyer. Then, I got to meet Graeme Sharp, plus 'Changy' the mascot elephant!

After photos on the pitch with my family, I was taken to the Everton changing room and was introduced to the likes of David Moyes, Phil Jagielka, Mikel Arteta and Leighton Baines.

Next, I was walking round the perimeter of the pitch, giving our Everton mints to the crowd - saving a few extra ones for my family (and, excitingly, a spare bag to take into school the next week).

Then came Z-Cars. The players came onto the pitch, and I was photographed at the handshake between captains Phil Neville and Martin Laursen from Villa.

We watched the match from the Family Enclosure, but it was a very cold afternoon, and the effects of my medication were wearing off, and dad took me home before the final whistle, so I can’t be blamed for the late Villa winning goal scored by Ashley Young! A few days later, I received a lovely set of photos of me with David Moyes and some of the players.

Although I don’t get to matches often, I remain an Evertonian and do my best to re-educate my Manchester United-supporting boyfriend. My sister Ceri never did have the honour of being Toffee Lady but remains ready and willing, if called upon!

By Siân Sawyer, Evertonian

My Everton shares first-hand accounts describing the most-treasured memories of fans, players, and staff both past and present.

#1270. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It’s back-to-back wins for Chelsea and a rare clean sheet, their first since January. But all thoughts will be with Emi Martinez after his clash of heads with Branthwaite. Hopefully we get some good news on that front soon. Follow the latest updates here.

Enzo Maresca has been looking for opportunities for rest his key players - but Erling Haaland is a player that is impossible to rest. He has scored in his last seven matches and leads Manchester City’s attack again.

But Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.

A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.

City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1268. HIBERNIAN 2 DUNDEE 1: Hibs enjoy some long lost home comfort as Leith men win the battle of the wounded

Published: 18:46 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 18:51 EST, 24 November 2026

Hibernian ended their long wait for a Premiership home win after overcoming Dundee in a hard-fought contest at Easter Road.

Martin Boyle and Nicky Cadden – who curled home a stunning effort from outside the box – had the hosts in command before the interval.

But Dundee, still licking their wounds after an 8-0 savaging at the hands of Hearts on Saturday, showed plenty of fight after the break and pulled one back through Joe Wright.

The visitors tried in vain to grab an equaliser and it was Hibs who were left satisfied by their first three points at home since beating Kilmarnock on April 4.

Manager Marink Reedijk was thrilled to have bounced back from their 4-0 weekend home defeat at the hands of Dundee United, saying: ‘I think it’s a good reaction to what we have done against Dundee United.

‘It’s important that you get the three points at home. Again, that’s a big win. I saw a front foot team again, I saw togetherness again, I saw a team who fought for every ball.

Martin Boyle takes the acclaim after scoring the all-important second goal for Hibernian

‘That’s not easy, they have to be patient, you have to be secure, you have to wait for your moment and we took these moments and that was really good to see.

‘The goal of Nicky [Cadden] is one to, we say, put in a frame and put on your wall as a painting. The one of Martin [Boyle] is why Martin is so important for us. He can disrupt an opponent if they are so organised and so close to each other and so deep.

‘As long as we keep ourselves, I think these are good signs.’

Hibs played on the front foot as they looked to start repairing the damage from the weekend. On a rare start, Togo international Thibault Klidje was lively and saw a header crash into the side-netting before hitting a harmless snap-shot straight at Dundee goalkeeper Owen Goodman.

From a short corner routine Hibs worked space for Cadden on the edge of the box from Josh Mulligan’s lay-off and his driving effort whistled just past a post.

Dundee were desperate to keep it tight at the back but offered little going forward. Just when it looked like they were beginning to settle Hibs hit them with two goals in three minutes before the break.

The first came in the 40th minute when Boyle fired a penalty past Goodman after being tripped by Ryan Finnigan.

Nicky Cadden unleashes an absolute pearler into the top corner to put Hibs in front

Cadden then found the top corner with a sublime curling effort from his left foot just outside the box. It was another short corner routine that saw Miguel Chaiwa set up the wing-back.

Despite the hammer blow of losing two goals in quick succession before the break, Dundee demonstrated at the start of the second half that they were not going to roll over.

Steven Pressley’s side upped their intensity as they searched for a goal to get themselves back in the game and that arrived in the 67th minute courtesy of Wright.

Substitute Callum Jones’ free-kick should have been put away by Ryan Astley but the ball broke back to Wright and he slammed the ball high into the net from six yards.

That set up a tense finish but Hibs desperately held on for a rare home victory.

For Pressley, who changed half of his outfield XI following his side’s weekend humiliation, there were also positives to take.

The Dark Blues boss said: ‘We’re disappointed to not come away with anything and to obviously lose the game. But I also thought we restored some degree of pride tonight.

‘Going into half-time 2-0 down, losing two late goals in the half, can be a little bit demoralising, especially for a team that has a bit of fragility on the back of the weekend’s result.

‘I thought we responded brilliantly. We showed a lot of courage, a lot of determination, a lot of spirit and, as I’ve said, I think we certainly restored some level of pride that allows us a foundation to move into the weekend.’

#1267. Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics1,2. Although the landscape of height-associated common genetic variation has been studied extensively2, rare variation remains relatively unexplored1. Here, using rare protein-altering variants in a discovery set of 826,066 exomes, we identify 207 height-associated genes, 98% of which replicate in an additional 624,567 individuals. The rarest and most deleterious class of variation, singleton (frequency < 0.0001%) putative loss-of-function variants, implicated 17 genes with large effects on height ranging from −17cm (ACAN) to +11 cm (FBN1) per allele, 52× larger than the average effect of common height-associated variants and comparable to the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score. Several genes (TET1, DTL and IGF2BP2) have effect sizes that are at least as large as established Mendelian height genes, yet lack documented stature or skeletal growth syndromes, particularly for genes associated with increased height. Our large-scale sequencing study elucidates the genetic architecture and allelic heterogeneity of rare variants in height, providing unique insights into their large effects—often similar to or larger than recognized Mendelian syndromes—and their impact on trait prediction, clinical evaluation, and discovery power to facilitate drug target prioritization.

Although height was described as a heritable trait as early as 18863, its genetic architecture started to emerge only in the late twentieth century when researchers began identifying the genetic causes of Mendelian syndromes with a substantial stature component4,5,6,7. Non-syndromic genetic modulators of height remained unclear until 2007, when genome-wide association studies (GWASs) identified the first common variants associated with height8. Fifteen years later, a GWAS of 5.3 million individuals identified 12,111 independent variants that collectively accounted for 40% of the variance in height across individuals of European descent2. As with other traits, height GWASs predominantly implicated common non-coding variants with modest effects (<1 cm)2, complicating efforts to link associations directly to specific genes and functional mechanisms.

By contrast, sequencing-based studies of rare variation can directly implicate causal genes by identifying large-effect putative loss-of-function (pLoF) and missense variants9. To systematically assess the contribution of rare coding variation to height, we performed a multiancestry exome sequencing analysis of adult height in 1,450,633 individuals across 12 cohorts (Supplementary Table 1), in which we (1) identified 17 height-associated genes through a burden of singleton pLoFs; (2) identified additional height-associated genes by including nonsynonymous variants up to 1% alternate allele frequency (AAF) and applying non-burden tests that do not assume variant effects act in the same direction; and (3) estimated the impact of rare protein-altering variation on genetic-based height prediction.

Using 826,066 individuals from six cohorts (Supplementary Table 1), we performed three discovery association analyses of adult height: (1) imputed common variants (AAF > 0.01); (2) rare exome variants (AAF ≤ 0.01, alternate allele count (AAC) ≥ 10); and (3) gene-based tests grouping rare coding variants. We used a single unified Bonferroni significance threshold of 1.75 × 10−9 across all three analyses (Methods). For gene-based analyses, we used a gene-wide omnibus statistic, gene-P10, that aggregates evidence across burden tests and two other gene-based tests, variant-level aggregate Cauchy association tests (ACAT-V)11 and optimal sequence kernel association tests (SKAT-O)12 (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1). We used six additional cohorts with 624,567 individuals for replication (Supplementary Table 1) and assessed the impact of rare variants on height prediction using a subset (n = 242,679).

Common variant analysis identified 3,034 conditionally independent height associations (Supplementary Table 2) that collectively explain around 25% of the observed variation in height (Methods and Supplementary Note). We conditioned on these 3,034 common variants to ensure rare variant and gene-based associations were independent of common variant signals (Supplementary Note and Supplementary Fig. 2). We identified 105 rare nonsynonymous variants in 87 genes (median AAF = 2.16 × 10−3; Supplementary Table 3) and 207 genes associated with height (gene-P < 1.75 × 10−9; Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 4). In total, 82 out of the 87 genes with significant rare nonsynonymous variant associations are also among the 207 genes identified through gene-based tests.

As singleton pLoFs represent the rarest and most deleterious class of variants, we first focused on this subset. Singleton pLoF burden tests identified 17 genes, 11 height decreasing and 6 height increasing, with a mean absolute effect of 8.92 cm per allele (Fig. 1, Table 1 and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6), about 52× larger than the average GWAS variant (\(\overline{|{\beta }_{\mathrm{GWAS}}|}\) = 0.17 cm) and around 44× larger (range 14.4× to 78.3×) when comparing effects per gene (Methods and Supplementary Table 7). Effects ranged from a 16.6-cm decrease in stature for ACAN singleton pLoF carriers to an 11.1-cm increase in stature for FBN1 singleton pLoF carriers. The effect of carrying a singleton pLoF in one of these 17 genes approaches the cumulative effect observed in the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score (PGS) (top 1%, +9.60 cm; bottom 1%, −9.12 cm; Fig. 2a, Methods and Supplementary Tables 8 and 9). These incredibly rare pLoFs, cumulatively carried by fewer than 0.1% of individuals (744 carriers among 826,066 individuals), have a larger impact on height than all but the most extreme combinations of common variants.

Inside each point is the number of genes discovered (top) and the absolute mean effect (in centimetres; bottom). Effect sizes were estimated by multiplying β by the s.d. of observed height (about 7.99 cm). All P values are two-sided, calculated by REGENIE in discovery analysis (n = 826,066), and significance assessed using a P-value threshold of 1.75 × 10−9.

These 17 genes belong to well-established biological processes and pathways affecting height, including extracellular matrix organization and skeletal/growth pathways such as growth hormone/insulin-like growth factor (GH/IGF), WNT/β-catenin and transforming growth factor-β1,13,14,15 (TGFβ) (Table 1 and Extended Data Table 1).

Incorporating more common variation into burden tests can increase statistical power for gene discovery by adding variant carriers, although at the cost of attenuated effect sizes. Expanding our analysis to include increasingly frequent pLoFs, followed by including missense variants, identified an additional 162 genes (Extended Data Fig. 1).

Among pLoFs, relaxing the burden test AAF threshold from singletons (about 0.00006%) to 1% identified 76 genes, 62 not discovered with pLoF singletons alone. On average, burden tests aggregating more common pLoFs had a 3.96-cm effect—less than half the 8.92-cm effect of pLoF singletons, but still 24× larger than the average GWAS association (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 10). Among the 15 genes with pLoF singleton associations that remained significant at AAF < 0.01%, we observed a 35% attenuation in the absolute effect size (from 8.71 cm to 5.68 cm), suggesting that a substantial fraction of more frequent pLoF-annotated variants may not cause complete loss of function. Two genes—CHD8 (associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability) and COL1A1 (associated with Ehlers–Danlos syndrome16 and osteogenesis imperfecta)—were identified only through singleton pLoF burden tests. When more frequent pLoFs were included, burden test effect sizes fell by 78% for COL1A1 and 83% for CHD8 and were no longer statistically significant (Fig. 1a). By contrast, three genes with absolute effects on height of >1 s.d. (7.99 cm) reached significance only with higher-frequency pLoFs: SHOX17 in the fibroblast growth factor pathway (β = −12.05 cm, P = 2.85 × 10−16); transcriptional regulator ERF (β = −8.67 cm, P = 4.41 × 10−21); and HMGA2, the insulin-like growth factor pathway gene underlying the first height GWAS discovery8 (β = −8.11 cm, P = 6.11 × 10−13). These three genes each had few singleton pLoFs (1, 6, and 16 carriers, respectively); aggregating singletons with additional rare pLoFs was therefore essential to achieve significance.

This expanded set of height-associated pLoF burden genes highlighted additional canonical growth pathways and height biology (for example, the fibroblast growth factor pathway; Extended Data Table 1), as well as additional members from the same gene families and pathways implicated by pLoF singleton genes (Supplementary Table 11).

Whereas pLoFs represent the rarest and most deleterious class of coding variation, missense variants represent the most frequent class of protein-altering variants9,18,19. If missense variants ablate protein function to a similar extent as pLoFs, we might expect both increased statistical power and similar effect sizes when combining both in burden tests. Conversely, if missense variants only partially diminish protein function or exert opposing effects through gain-of-function (GoF) mechanisms, burden effect sizes will be attenuated.

We combined pLoFs with three sets of missense variants: (1) all missense variants; (2) missense variants inconsistently classified as deleterious by in silico algorithms (possibly deleterious); and (3) missense variants confidently classified as deleterious by in silico algorithms (deleterious; Methods), collectively identifying 154 genes (85 not discovered by pLoFs alone; Fig. 1c). When combined with pLoF variants, successively filtering rare missense variants for increasing deleteriousness increased discovery power, yielding 96, 116, and 132 genes for each of the above groups, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Among the 14 genes with both significant singleton pLoF and singleton pLoF + deleterious missense burden associations (Table 1), the absolute effect size decreased 28.5% on average when adding deleterious missense singletons (8.70 cm versus 6.22 cm; Fig. 1b). This observation holds broadly across height-associated genes, with diminished pLoF + missense effect sizes reflecting both that missense variants account for most rare allele carriers (68.5% in singleton and 84.1% in AAF < 1% burden tests) and that the effect of missense variants is, on average, substantially smaller than that of pLoFs (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 10). Despite diminished effect sizes, the higher allele counts contributed by missense variants substantially increased overall discovery power, more than doubling the number of associated height genes.

Of the 85 genes not discovered by pLoFs alone, UHRF2 (singleton pLoF + deleterious missense variants: β = −4.74 cm, P = 3.6 × 10−12)—an E3 ubiquitin ligase regulating the cell cycle20—and PTPN11 (pLoF + deleterious missense variants AAF < 0.01%: β = −4.00 cm, P = 2.5 × 10−32)—a signalling protein involved in development and hormone response through the RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT signalling pathways21—had the largest effect sizes.

We found six genes (ESR1, FGFR3, HSD11B2, MTMR11, PTPN11 and RPL5) that exhibited the strongest association from missense-only burden tests, and pLoF burden tests were, at best, only nominally significant (Supplementary Table 13). Four genes (FGFR3, HSD11B2, PTPN11 and RPL5) had opposite directions of effect between pLoF and missense burden tests, although the pLoF estimates were not statistically significant. Notably, three genes—FGFR3 (refs. 7,22), PTPN11 (ref. 23) and ESR1 (ref. 24)—have previously reported GoF mutations that drive syndromic conditions with notable skeletal growth phenotypes, including achondroplasia (FGFR3)22 and Noonan syndrome (PTPN11)23. Given the known GoF mechanisms for three of these genes, the other missense-driven genes may also affect height through GoF mechanisms.

The new genes identified by incorporating missense variants further underscore previously implicated pathways, biological functions and gene families (Supplementary Table 11) but also implicate different pathways (for example, Sonic Hedgehog signalling) and biological processes, including sex hormone regulation and carbohydrate transport, storage and metabolism (Extended Data Table 1).

Although burden tests identified 179 height-associated genes (Extended Data Fig. 1a), they were not designed to identify genes of which variants with effects exist in opposite directions or where most variants have no effect. For these situations, SKAT-O12 and ACAT-V11 were developed.

Collectively, ACAT-V and SKAT-O identified 28 genes not detected by burden tests (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Before conditional analysis, ACAT-V and SKAT-O associations were more likely than burden test associations to be driven by linkage disequilibrium with common variants (Supplementary Note, Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 12). Consistent with the underlying model, SKAT-O associations highlight genes harbouring variants with opposing effects on height. For example, in PTCH1, a transmembrane protein receptor involved in Hedgehog signalling25, the SKAT-O association (P = 1.94 × 10−15) was driven by two variants: a missense variant associated with increased height (9:95458026G>A; p.T1052M; β = +1.00 cm, P = 4.8 × 10−11; Supplementary Table 3) and a splice acceptor variant associated with decreased height (9:95485875C>T; β = −4.28 cm, P = 1.9 × 10−9). Meanwhile, ACAT-V identified genes like FBN2 (P = 1.72 × 10−12), a component of microfibrils that stores and regulates growth factors including TGFβ26, in which the association was driven by one significant missense variant (5:128332993G>T; p.H1381N; β = +1.07 cm, P = 9.8 × 10−14; AAF = 0.48%; Supplementary Table 3).

Although gene-based tests are useful for boosting rare variant discovery power, we identified 121 significant rare (AAF < 1%) exome variants after conditioning on common GWAS variants (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Tables 3 and 14 and Supplementary Note). Of these 121 variants, 105 were nonsynonymous (85 missense, 17 pLoFs and 3 in-frame insertions or deletions (indels)) and implicated 87 genes, 82 of which overlapped genes implicated by gene-based tests (60 from burden tests; 22 genes from ACAT-V or SKAT-O).

For the 82 genes identified by both single variants and gene-based tests, we compared the consistency of effect sizes between burden test and significant individual variants (Methods). Focusing on the 79 rare nonsynonymous variants (59 missense, 17 pLoFs, 3 in-frame indels) in 60 genes with a significant burden test, we found that 52 (66%) had larger effect sizes than the largest burden test effect. The neurodevelopmental-disorder-associated gene KMT2B27 had the largest discrepancy, with a nearly 20-fold difference between variant 19:35720959C>T (p.R538C; β = −7.67 cm, P = 2.6 × 10−10, AAF = 2.61 × 10−5) and the largest burden test effect (β = −0.38 cm, P = 5.0×10−10; pLoF and possibly deleterious missense variants with AAF < 0.01%).

Two genes with GoF missense variants, FGFR3 and PTPN11, have multiple missense variants with some of the largest observed effects on height (Fig. 2b). Among the six exome-wide significant variants in FGFR3, a pathogenic GoF missense variant causing achondroplasia7 (4:1804392G>A; p.G380R; P = 3.22 × 10−64) decreases height by 29.78 cm, about 13× larger than the largest FGFR3 burden test effect (β = −2.31 cm, P = 2 × 10−41; deleterious missense variants AAF < 0.0001; Extended Data Fig. 2). PTPN11 also contains two significant pathogenic GoF missense variants23,28: p.R265Q (12:112472981G>A; β = −12.26 cm, P = 6 × 10−19) and p.N308D (12:112477719A>G; β = −14.21 cm, P = 4 × 10−14), with effects around 3× larger than the largest burden signal (β = −4.12 cm, P = 3.6 × 10−33; deleterious missense variants with AAF < 0.0001). These examples emphasize the challenge that allelic heterogeneity presents for interpreting and using gene-level burden effect sizes. We discuss the implications of effect size heterogeneity on phenotypic prediction below (see the ‘Heritability, enrichment and prediction’ section).

Recent studies29,30 demonstrated that non-additive models can identify associations missed by standard approaches; we therefore tested rare coding variants under a recessive model. This identified only one association missed by additive tests: the CFTR ΔF508 mutation that causes cystic fibrosis31 was not associated with height under an additive model (βadd = −0.05 cm; Padd = 0.14), but was associated with a 5.87-cm height reduction in homozygotes in the recessive model (Prec = 5 × 10−10; replication and additional details are provided in the Supplementary Note). This result is consistent with both the recessive nature of cystic fibrosis mutations and the established impact of cystic fibrosis on growth and stature. The inability of cystic fibrosis treatments to fully restore growth trajectory and stature, along with diminished IGF1 levels exhibited by newborns with cystic fibrosis, are findings compatible with a direct effect of CFTR on height through fetal and/or neonatal growth pathways32,33.

We sought to understand the differences in genetic architecture across genetic ancestry groups by stratifying single-variant and gene-based tests by ancestry (Methods). Consistent with previous findings, we detected no effect-size heterogeneity by genetic ancestry34. However, we identified several ancestry-specific signals resulting from differences in AAF and sample size. Most associations specific to a single ancestry were identified in the European subset, which accounts for most participants (n = 640,240, 78%; Supplementary Table 15 and Supplementary Note). One notable exception is a rare HHIP p.V496E substitution associated with decreased height exclusively in the admixed American subpopulation (AMR AAF = 0.05%, P = 1.52 × 10−9, β = −3.96 cm; Supplementary Table 15 and Supplementary Note). This variant is observed only in individuals from the Mexico City Prospective Study35. We speculate that the p.V496E variant is a GoF missense variant, as rare HHIP pLoFs appear to be associated with increased height (pLoF singleton β = +9.92 cm, P = 3.72 × 10−7). Similarly, we replicate a known signal at a FBN1 missense variant36 (p.E1297G; β = −2.12 cm, P = 2.9 × 10−17; Supplementary Table 16) that is substantially more common in admixed Americans (about 1% versus 0.004% in Europeans) and occurs almost exclusively on Indigenous haplotypes (Supplementary Fig. 4). These discoveries underscore the value of sequencing diverse populations.

Height GWASs14 have consistently observed enrichment of Mendelian syndrome genes among height-associated common variant loci37; we observed similar enrichment in genes implicated through rare variation. Forty-three out of 76 genes (57%) with significant pLoF burden signals at AAF < 1% and 102 out of 207 (49%) height-associated genes in total were documented in the Mendelian syndrome in Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database, significantly more than expected by chance (odds ratio (OR) = 4.46, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 2.76–7.26, P = 1.83 × 10−10; Fisher’s exact test). Of the 43 Mendelian genes, 21 had annotated stature or skeletal growth features2, an 8.37-fold enrichment (95% CI = 4.34–16.10, P = 2.56 × 10−10; Fisher’s exact test). Genes with pLoF burden height associations and a Mendelian syndrome listed in OMIM are over 5× more likely to be associated with decreased height (36 out of 43, 83%). Among the 11 pLoF singleton genes with height-decreasing effects, 9 were in OMIM and 8 list stature or skeletal growth among the clinical characteristics. By contrast, among the six with height-increasing effects, three are in OMIM, but only FBN1 includes height among the clinical characteristics. Our results were insufficient to determine whether increased height is under-reported as a syndromic feature or whether genes leading to increased height are less likely to cause other clinical features and therefore cause fewer recognized syndromes (Supplementary Note).

Previous studies estimated that the gene nearest to a GWAS peak is the causal gene in around 70% of instances9,38. We observed strong overlap between large-effect rare variant burden associations and GWAS peaks, although this overlap diminishes noticeably with the stringency of the burden definition and variant frequency. Of pLoF singleton genes, 82% (14 out of 17) are the closest gene to a GWAS peak, compared with only 60% (92 out of 154) of pLoF + missense burden genes. In total, 28 out of 207 genes are not among the top 10 nearest genes to any common variant signal. Notably, 4 genes are >1 Mb from the nearest common variant association signal: FIBIN, HHIPL1, PTPN11 and WLS. Even compared with the 12,111 index variants from ref. 2, PTPN11 is not among the 10 nearest genes to any GWAS peak, with the closest signal 393 kb away (Supplementary Table 4).

To assess the validity of our results, we performed replication analyses in six independent cohorts comprising an additional 624,567 individuals (Supplementary Table 1). Despite the 24.4% smaller sample size, 203 out of 207 (98.1%) genes and 113 out of 125 (90.4%) single variants replicated with nominal significance (α = 0.05; Methods, Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 and Supplementary Note), demonstrating both high consistency of height associations and the robustness of our Bonferroni threshold. Furthermore, replication rates were consistent across gene-based tests—BURDEN-ACAT, 98.1% (155 out of 158); SBAT, 93.8% (166 out of 177); SKAT-O, 95.3% (164 out of 172); and ACAT-V, 94.9% (94 out of 99; Supplementary Fig. 5b–e). Replication performance for single variants improved to 96.1% (98 out of 102) after restricting to variants with over 80% estimated replication power (Supplementary Fig. 5f). Irrespective of power, all 179 burden genes and all but one variant had consistent directions of effect between discovery and replication analyses (Supplementary Note). Furthermore, gene-based tests maintained high replication rates well above our study-wide P-value threshold (Supplementary Note and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). For example, 91.6% of the 368 genes reaching a discovery gene-P < 2.5 × 10−6—roughly equivalent to one test per gene—replicated with nominal significance (P < 0.05) and would implicate an additional 137 genes compared to our experiment-wide Bonferroni threshold (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Replication rates for single variants and singleton burden tests declined similarly, requiring respective P-value thresholds of 4 × 10−6 and 1 × 10−6 to achieve a comparable 91.6% replication rate when restricted to tests with over 80% power (Supplementary Figs. 5f and 6).

Finally, because burden tests were more likely to have negative (height-decreasing) effect estimates, we compared the ratio of effect directions across significance thresholds (Supplementary Note and Extended Data Fig. 3). The excess of height-decreasing burden effects persists well below the Bonferroni significance threshold, with the degree of imbalance varying by both significance threshold and variant class. These patterns suggest considerable rare variant signal yet to be discovered.

Rare variants are frequently offered as an answer to the ‘missing heritability’ problem in complex trait genetics39. Here we estimated the cumulative impact of rare coding variation on height at the population level by calculating the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to burdens of rare coding variants and assessing the potential of large-effect height-associated coding variants to improve height predictions.

First, burden heritability regression40 estimated the burden of rare nonsynonymous variants explain 3.97% (95% CI = 3.77–4.17%) of phenotypic variance (Extended Data Fig. 4, Supplementary Table 17 and Supplementary Note), nearly identical to the previously published estimate of 3.82% (95% CI = 3.55–4.09%)40. pLoFs with AAF < 0.001% accounted for the largest fraction of burden heritability, consistent with the large effects we observed for these extremely rare, damaging variants. This probably underestimates the true contribution of rare coding variants because the burden approach underestimates heritability in the presence of effect size heterogeneity40. Together, the most significant burden test for each of the 179 burden genes explains around 1.1% of phenotypic variance in the replication data, nearly 30% of the total estimated contribution of the burden of rare variants to adult height (Extended Data Fig. 5).

We next tested for enrichment of rare, deleterious variants in individuals whose height was poorly predicted by common variants in our replication data (n = 242,679), as rare variants unaccounted for in common variant prediction may contribute to the discrepancy between observed and genetically predicted height41,42,43. Individuals deviating from their common variant predicted height by >2.5 s.d. (±17–20 cm) were 17.2-fold (95% CI = 9.89–28.34, P = 1.12 × 10−16, Fisher’s exact test) enriched for carrying a singleton pLoF in one of the 17 singleton pLoF genes (Fig. 3a, Methods and Supplementary Table 18). By contrast, individuals at the extreme ends of the height distribution (>2.5 s.d.) were only 4.9-fold enriched (P = 1.89 × 10−7, Fisher’s exact test; Supplementary Table 19 and Supplementary Note) for pLoF singletons in these genes, consistent with previous results42,43.
