#1206. Saliba has fight on his hands to usurp ‘unbelievable’ Konsa

From the moment Ezri Konsa pulled on an Arsenal shirt, he has moved with all the composure of a man who knows exactly where to be and when. The centre-back has required no adaptation period in north London, where he has filled the considerable shoes of William Saliba with such class that Arsenal have hardly missed the Frenchman at all.

The loss of Saliba to a long-term back injury was supposed to be a major problem for Arsenal. Instead, the situation has now reached a point where some fans are wondering how Saliba will get back into the side. That may prove a little extreme, but the fact there is even a discussion is proof of Konsa’s superb impact at the Emirates Stadium.

“Unbelievable,” Mikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, said of his £55m signing. “He’s come to a huge club and to position yourself in that manner, and to perform at the level he is, it is very difficult to do. We are really lucky to have him.”

In Arsenal’s latest victory, their seventh from eight matches in the Premier League this season, Konsa offered all of his usual defensive security and calmness in possession. Even more excitingly, he also scored his first goal for the club, smashed in from close range after a corner had caused chaos in Everton’s penalty area. It was Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

“I have been waiting to score my first goal for a while,” Konsa said. “I spoke to the set-piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well. We felt as players that it was coming, and today was the day.”

Some eyebrows were raised when Arsenal paid such a large fee to sign Konsa from Aston Villa. The Villa fans, though, were not among those who questioned the price or the player’s ability. They have known for years at Villa Park that Konsa is a player of the highest quality, and they will not be surprised by his exceptional start to his Arsenal career.

The same is true of the Arsenal players. Arteta asked the England internationals in his squad about Konsa before buying him, and the feedback was overwhelmingly positive. Konsa was already close friends with Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze before completing his transfer from Villa.

Konsa’s start to life at Arsenal is all the more impressive because he did not even have a pre-season. He effectively came straight from the World Cup into the club, and has been starting games since early September. His first start was against Chelsea, when he endeared himself to the home fans with a crunching tackle on former team-mate Morgan Rogers.

Konsa, 29, has quickly built a strong relationship with Gabriel Magalhães, his defensive partner who scored Arsenal’s other goal here against Everton, from Ben White’s cross. For both centre-backs to find the net felt like a throwback to last year, when Arsenal were so dangerous from crosses, and underlined how Arteta’s team are capable of hurting their opponents in many different ways.

The nature of the goals might give a misleading impression of Arsenal’s performance, though. This was not a gritty win. Arteta’s side produced some excellent passing moves and circulated the ball with menace throughout the game. They were also a little open at times, especially in the first half when Everton created a handful of decent chances.

Thierno Barry missed the best of those opportunities, with the score at 1-0. It was the closest the visitors came to hurting the champions, aside from some of James Tarkowski’s full-blooded tackles. “I felt we didn’t really get to a level that was good enough to get near them,” admitted David Moyes, the Everton manager.

The victory, combined with Manchester City’s defeat earlier in the day, put Arsenal level on points at the top of the table. Aside from the extraordinary thrashing at Brighton, Arteta’s side have looked just as solid, if not more so, than last season. That speaks volumes of the quality in the team, of course, but also says plenty about the way Konsa has adjusted to his new surroundings. Thanks to him, Saliba’s absence has not hurt at all.

“Great feeling, it always is. A clean sheet, a goal – my first goal for the club – so a fantastic day overall.

“I’ve been waiting to score my first goal for a while. I spoke to the set piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well, so it was only right that I got the goal today.

“I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us. It’s not surprising to me.

“We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”

All over at the Emirates and the champions go level on points with Manchester City at the top of the table.

They kept another clean sheet and scored from a set-piece again. All is right in Arsenal’s world!

Oscar Bobb’s first Premier League goal for Fulham earned a 1-0 win over Coventry that lifted the Cottagers clear of the relegation zone.

Bobb produced a fine bit of individual skill to strike in the 80th minute as he twisted his way into the box and bent a shot into the far corner, only his second goal for the club in any competition since his £27million move from Manchester City back in January.

That was enough to give Fulham their first away win in nine attempts, a run that dated back to February, only a week after they ended their winless start to the league campaign by edging out Hull 1-0 as the pressure continues to ease on Alvaro Arbeloa.

Josh King had earlier hit the post for the visitors, who edged Coventry in just about every department to leave Frank Lampard’s side second-bottom of the table.

The hosts had only brief spells of sustained possession in Fulham’s half, but did little to trouble Bernd Leno on a frustrating afternoon which bought the CBS Arena back down to earth after their 4-1 win over Newcastle in their last home outing.

Odegaard drives a shot high over the ball as Arsenal close in on another clean sheet.

Probably sums up Zubimendi’s season so far that he finally gets some meaningful minutes in the Premier League and ends up getting smashed in the face and covered in his own blood. This is after he got injured in a cool-down a few weeks ago. When your luck’s out...

Brilliant play from Oscar Bobb as he cuts inside on his left foot and bends a shot into the far bottom corner for the away side.

Treatment is needed for Zubimendi after he is caught on the nose by Barry.

Big chance for Everton. Garner whips a teasing cross into the box, Dewsbury-Hall meets it with his head on the run but the ball flies just wide of the post.

Tarkowski is the latest yellow card for Everton after a foul on Havertz.

Eze with a poor cross into the box. He fails to run back quickly and Arteta sprints to the edge of the touchline and goes berserk at the midfielder.

How have Arsenal reacted to their top scorer Saka being injured? Both of their centre backs have scored for the first time this season.

On his 200 Premier League appearance for Arsenal, Gabriel marks it with his first goal of the season.

It is a lovely move with slick one-touch passing. The ball is fed to White making a run down the outside and he clips the ball to the far post for Gabriel to head home.

OFF Merino, Lewis-Skelly, GyokeresON Calafiori, Guimaraes, Havertz

Garner is booked for Everton now after barging into Merino off the ball.

Arteta is shown a yellow card for something. Not sure what for yet. But the Arsenal manager is looking to make some changes off the bench.

Arsenal have been guilty of overplaying today. Opting for the extra pass rather than taking a shot. The game is open at the moment and that makes things dangerous for the home side.

Yellow card for Lewis-Skelly after bringing down Johnson. Gabriel is back on the pitch and seems happy enough to continue.

Arsenal have defensive options in Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori and Mosquera if Arteta wants to avoid taking any risks.

A worry for Arsenal as Gabriel jars his knee into the ground as he tries to clear the ball. The Brazilian is receiving treatment and hobbles off the pitch.

Gabriel immediately raised his hand for medical attention after making that clearance. He really extended his leg to get the ball away. Looks to be in a lot of pain.

Latest corner from Arsenal after Eze’s shot is blocked by Rohl. Rice’s delivery into the near post is headed clear to Odegaard, who shoots ambitiously from distance and Pickford collects the ball comfortably.

Arsenal get the match restarted. The longer the match goes on without extending the lead, Everton will think they have a chance.

Before today, Arsenal had averaged five corners per match in the Premier League this season. In the first 45 minutes here, they had 10 corners.

Yellow card for Mykolenko after he catches White wide on the right. Rice whips the ball in and Merino meets it with a flick goalwards but the ball goes over the bar.

That is the final touch of the half and the players are running off to get dry!

Big chance for Everton. White thinks he has time when he heads the ball back to Raya but he does not connect well and Barry is there to pick it up and he flicks a shot at goal but Raya reacts quickly to parry the ball.

Raya is penalised for taking too long with the ball and Everton have a cheap corner. Danger is cleared by Arsenal as they force Everton back into their half.

The conditions are terrible at the moment. Heavy wind and rain causing havoc.

A lot of set-pieces for Arsenal today as they continue to put Everton under the cosh. Can they take advantage of their dominance again before the break?

Arsenal have found their groove again, with Madueke twice going close to extending their lead. Rice, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard and Merino are forming a box in midfield and Everton don’t seem to know how to shut them down.

Another effort at goal for Madueke. This one is a snapshot from the edge of the box that goes into the side netting.

Madueke should do better. Rice finds him and the winger drives into the box. He takes a shot but drags a right-footed effort wide.

Chance for Arsenal. Rice finds space behind the Everton midfield and drives forward. He plays a pass to Lewis-Skelly, who lays it off to Eze. The England midfielder sidefoots a cross into the box but no one in an Arsenal shirt is there to meet it.

Courtesy of Opta: Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal in all competitions (not including penalties) since May of last season against Crystal Palace, ending a run of 13 games without one.

George is looking lively for Everton. He tries to come inside and whip an effort to the far corner but the ball deflects wide.

From the corner, Gabriel clears off the line after Raya loses track of the ball.

Everton have responded impressively to the Konsa goal and have been the better team since falling behind. Midfielders Garner and Armstrong are growing into the game quite nicely.

Everton have responded well to going behind here. The early goal against them will have ripped up any plans to sit deep and play on the counter.

Set-pieces are back on the menu for Arsenal. Ezri Konsa’s first goal for the club is their first goal from a corner this season, which will come as a relief to set-piece coach Nicolas Jover. “Set piece again, ole ole,” sing the Arsenal fans. Arteta’s side had started the game on the front foot.

Arsenal had not scored from a corner this season... until now. Konsa breaks the deadlock after a melee in the box and his pokes the ball into the net.

A couple of early set pieces from Declan Rice. Everton do well to clear the danger. But have another one now...

Horrible conditions at the Emirates today. The rain has been lashing down. The Emirates drainage system is usually able to cope with this sort of thing. If the wind picks up, that’s likely to be a bigger problem for the two teams.

After a minute’s applause in honour of Ken Friar, the match makes a prompt start at the Emirates.

“Yeah, we’ve had a good start. Obviously, we had a bit of a blip last week against Chelsea. I don’t think we, as a team, won first and second balls enough and that’s something the manager wants us to get back to today. You’ve got to win your battles.”

On what makes Arsenal difficult to play...

“They’re reigning Premier League champions, a top side that has been knocking on the door to win the title for a few years before as well. They’re a team at a high level but this is what Premier League football is all about and it’s up to us to get a result.”

“Well, we play every two-and-a-half days so we didn’t have much time to recover, so we need full energy. There are certain specific players as well that they fit really well for the game that we expect today and that’s how we start.”

“A very competitive team, a really well organised team. I think that it’s very clear what they want to do, where they want to take the game. The threats, when they have a space to run, any time that they are able to put the ball in their box, you know the presence and aggression that they have. So, yeah, we have to really be at it and be very aggressive from the beginning.”

One of the clearest signs a football club is in a good place is when the debate switches from whether the team are winning to how they are winning.

This is currently Arsenal and Mikel Arteta’s world. For years, Arsenal coaches and players were asked how and when they would start collecting major trophies again. With no concern about their capacity to challenge for top honours over the coming years, the style has become the main focus.

It’s a welcome “problem” – or some might argue a non-existent one – for Arteta while his side is so strong. Building a fortress is the expensive, time-consuming and difficult part. Once it’s constructed and established, how you decorate it is a matter of taste.

Whether neutrals will hold the current champions in the same regard as the great Arsène Wenger sides will be a trivial concern if Arteta does what no Arsenal manager has since 1935 – defend the league title – and then add a few more, which is a serious possibility based on the balance of power in England and the likely punishment heading Manchester City’s way.

Today there will be tributes to Ken Friar, who passed away at the age of 92 earlier this year. Advertising boards outside the Emirates Stadium have been taken over by images of Friar, who had a remarkable 70-year association with the club.

In today’s programme, captain Martin Odegaard has written the following: “It’s exceptional people like Ken Friar who have built the club into what it is today, and we as the current team are the ones privileged to continue his legacy.”

This is a first Premier League start of the season for Viktor Gyokeres, who has been behind Kai Havertz in the pecking order over the past few months. Gyokeres has yet to score in nine appearances in all competitions this season, although he would (understandably) make the point that it’s harder to do so when you are coming off the bench late in games.

For Arsenal, Arteta shuffles his team after the draw against Bayern: White, Lewis-Skelly, Merino, Eze and Gyokeres start.

Max Dowman, who scored a memorable goal in this fixture last season, is on the bench.

For Everton, Jack Grealish misses today’s game due to sickness, while Jarrad Branthwaite is absent because of concussion protocols despite finishing last week’s match with Chelsea after a head collision with Emi Martinez.

Arsenal: Raya, White, Gabriel, Konsa, Lewis-Skelly, Rice, Merino, Odegaard, Madueke, Eze, Gyokeres.Subs: Arrizabalaga, Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori, Mosquera, Zubimendi, Guimaraes, Dowman, Havertz

Everton: Pickford, Tarkowski, O’Brien, Armstrong, Rohl, Dewsbury-Hall, George, Barry, Garner, Mykolenko, JohnsonSubs: Travers, King, Maitland-Niles, Keane, Dibling, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney, Braiden Graham

Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

“I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes said: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

“When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

#1205. Celtic Could FInally Unlock Hassan by Signing Primary Target Ashour

Celtic are now being linked with a move for a new midfielder as they look to plug a key gap and wake summer signing Haissem Hassan out of his slump. A number of midfielders have been linked with a move to Parkhead ahead of the winter transfer window, and the newest name on the list is Al Ahly star Emam Ashour.

The Bhoys made some big mistakes in the summer transfer window, and chief among them was their failure to replace Arne Engels, who left on a £22million deal to join West Ham. Engels was one of the most pivotal cogs in the Celtic team last season, and after missing out on Champions League qualification, the Bhoys board cut back on spending and decided to go with what they had, with the exception of some cheap late signings that included youngster Joel van der Berg and loan signing Oliver Sorensen, who has struggled so far.]

But while Mika Baur has done a good job filling in playing in a deeper role, Celtic know they need more there, and they were given a harsh reminder when Baur was ruled out for 10 weeks with an ankle issue recently.

That has exposed a big gap, and Celtic know they need to recruit at the position this winter. Torino's Gvidas Gineitis has been linked after he was targeted in the summer, but now Al Ahly star Ashour is being linked.

Mark Hendry has reported that Ashour is Celtic's leading midfield target ahead of the winter, as someone who can play both ways in the midfield.

"Celtic interest remains in Emam Ashour, as I first reported back in July. They’ve always seen him as a No.8 who can operate in defensive role. Gvidas Gineitis also option but club considering next steps, including more discussions with Al-Ahly over Ashour." - Mark Hendry on X.

Ashour impressed for Egypt at the World Cup during the summer, and he was once described as a 'big quality player' by Tottenham star Omar Marmoush.

But what Ashour does in the midfield could be secondary to the impact he has with struggling winger Hassan. Hassan arrived at Parkhead on a £6million deal that could rise to £9million in the summer, although some of those add-ons were voided by the Hoops failing to qualify for the Champions League.

The 24-year-old dazzled for Egypt in the World Cup but with just two assists and no goals, he has flattered to deceive at Celtic. Hassan has plenty of quality, and it's clear when has the ball at his feet, but he is not doing enough, and Martin O;Neill knows it. Hassan should be beating Premiership defenders on repeat, but he is not reliably doing so, and it comes at the cost of being rather lazy defensively. O'Neill will likely put up with the lack of defensive effort if Hassan is running riot up top, but that simply isn't the case, and it has led Hassan to be omitted from the last two matchday squads. Although O'Neill said the last game was due to the winger having a longer international window and coming back later than most. Hassan will be involved on Thursday night against Torreense in the Europa League, but it's clear he has questions to answer, and while unverified, there have been murmurings of the winger not being particularly popular in the dressing room. O'Neill denied that. He said:

"Apparently something came out that he was the most unpopular player in the dressing room – which is not true. I didn’t say this."

What better way to spark Hassan's Celtic career to life than signing a midfielder he plays with and has performed well with on the international stage? And it would be a smart move to get both of them feeling comfortable in their surroundings, given they could lean on one another while they try to get going at Parkhead.

#1204. How Donnarumma reacted to Napoli fans’ insults in Man City’s ‘theatre-like’ stadium

La Gazzetta dello Sport reports that Napoli fans’ insults towards Gianluigi Donnarumma were clearly audible in the quiet stadium, prompting the Italy captain to respond during and after the game.

Napoli fans at the Etihad Stadium insulted Italy captain Donnarumma last night.

Around the hour mark, with Napoli in the lead, away supporters in the third tier started targeting the Italy national team captain with repeated insulting chants.

Gigio reacted by raising his hand, as if to say he had heard it but didn’t appreciate it. He made no rude gesture, but the chants continued.

When Napoli scored the second goal, going 2-1 up, chants became even louder.

The Gazzetta correspondent noted that chants were “easy to hear in Manchester City’s theatre-like stadium, where football tourism is commonplace on European nights.”

As Napoli fans continued to insult him and his mother, Donnarumma sarcastically invited them to keep going, suggesting that the chants didn’t really bother him. Gigio once again made it clear he had heard them, but kept his cool and avoided any rude gestures.

The Azzurri captain, however, didn’t hide his frustration as he left the stadium through the mixed zone later on, telling Napoli reporters he was upset by insults aimed at his mother.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

He’s our national team keeper, also, and arguably one of the best in the world.

Chants at his expense, if he makes a mistake, fine. Football fans will do that. But at his mother, that’s disgraceful. Have some respect, it’s distasteful and unnecessary…

Only losers target a mother or any family members, an exclusive LOSER attribute.

#1203. Pollock at heart of scuffle that inspires Leicester to thumping win in feisty derby

Henry Pollock was at the centre of an East Midlands derby flare-up that sparked a second-half Leicester onslaught as Northampton were overpowered at a sodden Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

The England back row, never knowingly far from controversy, escalated a brawl at the end of the first half that Leicester prop Joe Heyes revealed “added fuel to the fire” of a Tigers side who roared impressively when they returned after the break.

The incident fired up a sell-out crowd and Leicester brought what had up to that point been a drab game to life with a storming second-half performance.

Three tries in a pulverising 13-minute spell overturned a half-time deficit and put the hosts on course for a bonus-point win over their arch-rivals that took them to second place in the Prem table.

Pollock, withdrawn after 52 minutes, may wish to reflect on the wisdom of riling the Tigers in their own lair.

“That was a proper Tigers second half and a really pleasing performance,” Geoff Parling, their director of rugby, said.

“We got on the front foot and showed our power. The way the guys problem-solved was brilliant and I’m just really pleased with the emotional energy they threw into that game.

“The way we were physically for each other – I’m really pleased.

“The challenge for us, if we want to be a title-winning team, is to play like that when it isn’t Northampton Saints. We have to play with that heart – the fire we showed in our chests – but also the calmness we showed too.

“I think if we play our game to the best of our ability we can knock over anyone.”

It was a chastening afternoon for the champions who last won at Welford Road in January 2023.

Phil Dowson, Saints’ director of rugby, felt his side were in the contest at the interval but bemoaned the fact that they were unable to handle Leicester’s second-half power surge.

“It was a scrap. The conditions were going to dictate that. And they had some set-piece dominance which hurt us,” he said.

“That gave them a ton of energy and we didn’t seem able to respond, which was probably the most disappointing thing.

It’s a big day for Alex Coles, who celebrates his milestone 150th cap today.

The 27-year-old lock follows Fraser Dingwall, Rory Hutchinson and Alex Mitchell to become the fourth member of Saints’ current squad to reach 150 appearances for his boyhood club, eight years after making his debut in 2018.

Coles marks one of nine changes to Saints’ side for the Derby Day clash, with Emmanuel Iyogun, Curtis Langdon, Ed Prowse, Tom Pearson and Henry Pollock the other names coming into the forward pack.

Cleopas Kundiona retains his place in the front row while milestone man Coles joins Prowse in the second row against Tigers.

Josh Kemeny, with the 27-year-old continues at blindside flanker while Tom Pearson is set to make his first Prem appearance of the season.

Northampton Saints: J Pater; T Freeman, R Hutchinson, F Dingwall, G Hendy; F Smith, A Mitchell, E Iyogun, C Langdon, C Kundiona, A Coles, E Prowse, J Kemeny, T Pearson, H Pollock.

Replacements: R Smith, D Fischetti, I Neculai, JJ Van Der Mescht, T Lockett, C Chick, A McParland, O Sleightholme.

Parling has made five changes from the side that endured a 41-17 defeat to Pau.

Solomone Kata returns from injury to start at inside centre, with Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Jack van Poortvliet also coming into the backline to replace Ollie Hassell-Collins and Tom Whiteley respectively.

In the pack, Joe Heyes joins Archie van der Flier and Jamie Blamire who retain their places in the front row, while the second row make up of Cameron Henderson and Ollie Chessum remains unchanged.

Aaron Wainwright comes back into the starting lineup in the back row, with Finn Carnduff moving to openside flanker, with Olly Cracknell going at No 8.

Leicester: F Steward; A Radwan, W Wand, S Kata; G Hamer-Webb; B Searle, J van Poortvliet; A van der Flier, J Blamire, J Heyes, C Henderson, O Chessum, A Wainwright, F Carnduff, O Cracknell.

Replacements:  R Asiata, T Haffar, W Hurd, J Thompson, J Moro, T Whiteley, O Bailey, G Pearson.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the new campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

#1202. Johnny Giles Named English Legend as ‘Best Player I Ever Played Against’

Active from the late 1950s until the mid-1980s, Johnny Giles, whose real name is Michael Jones Giles, enjoyed an outstanding career. His achievements extended beyond being an exceptional football player, as he also made his mark in management.

The midfielder began his professional journey at Manchester United, where he lifted the 1963 FA Cup, before making the switch to Leeds United, where he spent 12 hugely successful years. At Elland Road, the Dublin-born star became an integral part of the Whites' team, collecting several major honours, including two league titles. He also earned a reputation as one of the toughest players in Leeds United's history.

A hugely talented footballer, Giles also represented the Republic of Ireland, taking on the role of player-manager in 1973. He scored 59 times (five goals) between 1959 and 1979. It was an unusual responsibility, but one that suited the Boys in Green icon, who also enjoyed spells with West Bromwich Albion and Shamrock Rovers.

Throughout such an illustrious career, Giles naturally shared the pitch with many of the finest footballers of his generation. However, one particular English legend stood out above the rest and left a lasting impression on him.

Speaking to Off The Ball, Giles revealed that he regarded Sir Bobby Charlton as the finest opponent he ever encountered on the pitch. It would hardly be surprising if the former midfielder also considered him among the best players he shared a team with. Giles described Charlton's abilities:

"He was the best player I ever played against, he was quick, had a great shot on him on either foot. I never really spoke to him about football, I think he played instinctively and - I don't mean to be disrespectful - I don't think he knew much about the game. Bobby didn't need anybody, he could dribble, he was quick and good with both feet."

Before facing one another as opponents, Giles and Charlton enjoyed considerable success together at Manchester United. However, Giles' move to Leeds United changed their relationship on the pitch, with the pair subsequently meeting as rivals. Their respective international careers also brought them into direct competition. Interestingly, the Republic of Ireland midfielder enjoyed the better record in their encounters, winning eight of their 20 meetings, drawing eight and losing just four. Nevertheless, Charlton remained a formidable opponent on every occasion.

It is difficult to argue against Giles' assessment when considering the extraordinary ability of Charlton, one of the greatest footballers ever. The Irishman clearly admired his former colleague, having also included him in his all-time England XI. It was a fitting recognition of a player whose quality was impossible to overlook.

Former Ireland international John Giles has compiled his all-time XI of players who have played for Celtic and Rangers.

Ask any Manchester United supporter to name the greatest footballer in the club's history, and Bobby Charlton will almost certainly feature in the conversation. One thing that cannot be disputed is his status as the greatest English player in Manchester United's history. The legendary forward, one of the best English footballers of all time, earned that distinction through years of outstanding performances. Having turned professional in 1956, the Ashington-born star spent 17 seasons representing the Red Devils.

Across that period, Charlton registered 758 appearances and scored 249 goals​​​​​​, while also collecting an impressive range of individual and team honours. Among his greatest achievements were winning the World Cup and claiming the Ballon d'Or in 1966, making him one of the seven British Ballon d'Or winners. His playing career might easily have ended in tragedy following the Munich Air Disaster, but he survived the devastating incident with relatively minor injuries. He subsequently dedicated much of his life to remembering and honouring the Manchester United teammates who lost their lives that day.

Bobby Charlton Stats at Manchester United

x3 First Division, x1 FA Cup, x1 European Cup, x2 FA Charity Shields

#1201. Sensational Spurs storm Stamford Bridge as Palmer loses his head

So much for Xabi Alonso’s call for cool heads from his Chelsea players. Cole Palmer lost his and was sent off, while goalkeeper Mike Penders punched the ball into his own net to give Tottenham Hotspur a helping hand on their way to a second win at Stamford Bridge in 42 attempts.

This was hardly “the Battle of the Bridge”, but Chelsea blew up during a ridiculous 10-minute spell towards the end of a game in which Tottenham had bossed possession but not looked like scoring.

Palmer was lucky to stay on the pitch in the 70th minute, when he shoved his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes after the Tottenham midfielder had stopped him racing through with a foul and a handball.

Christopher Kavanagh, the referee, let him off with a yellow card, but 10 minutes later Palmer inexplicably gave Kavanagh no choice but to book him again and send him off, following a late challenge on substitute Conor Gallagher.

Palmer was just about the only Chelsea player not to have been sent off last season, but it seems that Alonso has not yet managed to deal with the club’s disciplinary problem.

Jordan Henderson had given Palmer a talking to at the end of the win at Everton in which the forward was booked. But he evidently did not heed the advice or the words of his manager.

Alonso had said he was confident his players could keep calm ahead of the game, but he got that wrong – along with his team selection and substitutions.

In between Palmer’s two bookings, Penders suffered his own moment of madness with a bizarre own goal on his league debut for Chelsea. The Belgian was standing in for Emi Martinez, who watched in disbelief from the home dug-out after undergoing surgery on his jaw.

Fernandes sent in a corner that Jan Paul van Hecke challenged for. Penders looked like the easy winner in that contest, but he got his punch horribly wrong and the ball spun backwards and over the goalline.

The Chelsea fans predictably booed Gallagher, a graduate of the club’s academy who at times even stood in as captain. The foul on Gallagher that earned Palmer his marching orders silenced the jeers and the Chelsea fans’ boos only returned at the final whistle for their own players.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has told Cole Palmer he must learn from his red card that contributed to his team’s London derby defeat by Tottenham Hotspur.

Tottenham head coach Roberto De Zerbi insisted Palmer should have seen red for shoving his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes. But, having got off with a yellow card, the Chelsea midfielder then fouled substitute Conor Gallagher.

“I haven’t seen them [the yellow cards] on TV, but as far as I have been told, he [the referee] probably got it right,” Alonso said. “So, for sure for Cole, but for everyone. We think [up until] now we haven’t received any red cards [this season] and we need to continue that way because we need to have this maturity to deal with difficult moments, when you have conceded 1-0, there was still 15-20 minutes to go, so we have to be calm. I need to check the action to talk with Cole, but it is one to learn for the future for sure.”

Asked if he thought Palmer should have been sent off for the first yellow card, De Zerbi, who was booked for his protests, replied: “Yep.”

Jordan Henderson had spoken to Palmer at the end of the previous week’s victory over Everton in which the forward could also have been booked for a second time and sent off.

But Alonso claimed he does not have any wider concerns about Palmer’s character. He said: “Today, for sure, yes, but it is not a [wider] concern. I think that Cole when he is focused on the game, when he is enjoying and today after the 1-0, it is a moment to keep calm, a moment to keep mature and for everyone.”

De Zerbi hailed his side’s character and claimed that Tottenham have “suffered enough” after two 17th-placed finishes and a slow start to the season until successive victories over Coventry City and Chelsea.

“We want to improve, improve and improve, to be better game by game, week by week. I think we have suffered enough,” De Zerbi said. “Changing the spirit of the group, changing the performance of the players, especially the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We played very well. Great individual performances, great collective performance because we played very well. And then we put something different than Tottenham, I think, in the last period. Different attitude, different relationships with the players, different group.”

Chelsea were without João Pedro because of an injury and Alonso is waiting to find out how long the striker will be out.

“We don’t know yet because he has a lot of fluid,” Alonso said. “So he felt it yesterday [Friday] and we need to wait probably until tomorrow [Sunday] to do the test and to know the whole situation and the whole seriousness of the injury. We will know soon enough.”

Confirmation of that change as Gallagher replaces the injured Maddison, who heads straight down the tunnel. There’s some boos for Gallagher on his return to his former employers.

James Maddison is forced off with an injury and is replaced by Conor Gallagher, who receives a mixed reception from his former fans 🔃 https://t.co/GSeXQQ3eoa

There’s a break in play as Maddison goes down without anyone around him and glumly sits on the floor. He just can’t stay fit. Former Chelsea captain Gallagher is getting ready to come on.

Palmer surges forward before tumbling to the floor, believing he was clipped by Mateus Fernandes. There’s half-hearted appeals from some Chelsea players for a free kick on the edge of Spurs’ penalty area, but the referee isn’t interested.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break. Will we be treated to a more exiting second half? Let’s hope so.

It’s half-time at Stamford Bridge in a game lacking chances and attacking threat. Tottenham came closest to scoring just before the half-hour mark, when Marmoush forced Penders into terrific save on his first Premier League start. At the other end, Palmers tested Kinsky with a whipped effort, which the Spurs goalkeeper parried away. There’s much to ponder for Chelsea boss Alonso, whose plan to start to without a recognised striker has underwhelmed, while De Zerbi will feel more encouraged by his side’s display.

Hato takes a quick, clever free kick and finds Pedro Neto, whose made a great run. The winger flashes a low, driven shot off the wet surface from a tight angle, but Kinsky is there to gather it.

Spurs come forward on the counter through Tel, Marmoush and Kudus. However, the attack seems to lack conviction and it ends with Mateus Fernandes’ arrowed cross harmlessly drifting out of play.

We’re still waiting for this game to explode into life. It’s lacked the normal drama and controversy that this fixture normally provides.

Chelsea come alive as Kinsky miscues his pass, giving the ball to Pedro Neto. Palmer and Rogers get involved in the attack and it ends with a placed Henderson shot, which Kinsky does well to parry away. Chelsea look most dangerous when Kinsky has the ball at his feet and gives it away. The Tottenham goalkeeper needs to be careful.

Spurs burst forward on the counter and threads a pass through to Tel. Penders rushes out to smother the winger’s one-on-one effort. The offside flag was up, but Penders still did well to make the intervention.

Massive chance for Tottenham. Robertson slides a low, pinpoint cross into Marmoush, who shoots first-time from close range. Penders is up to the challenge and makes a pivotal stop to parry it away.

Penders comes out of his box and unconvincingly intercepts a through ball over the top of Chelsea’s defence. His pass has no power, but luckily for the young goalkeeper, it lands at Lacroix’s feet.

Spurs aren’t playing with their usual inferiority complex at Stamford Bridge. They looking confident. Chelsea are yet to strike a rhythm. Tel darts into Chelsea’s box, but Pedro Neto tracks back and makes an important tackle.

Chelsea’s substitutes have just been handed fluffy white towels to keep themselves dry and warm. I want one.

Tel’s deep cross finds Kudus at the back stick. The Ghanaian bends a curling strike around the covering defender. However, the shot evades the far post. Tottenham can certainly be encouraged by their start to this game.

Lacroix denies Maddison with a brilliant sliding challenge to win a goal kick for Chelsea. Maddison was convinced it was a corner.

We just heard a rather loud “For f***s sake” from Chelsea set-piece coach Austin MacPhee. Given we’ve just had Storm Austen, it feels appropriate that the Scotsman is giving the players a battering.

Pedro Neto does excellently to dispossess Mateus Fernandes, allowing Rogers to tee up Palmer. The playmaker whips a fierce effort aimed for the far top corner, but Kinsky is there to make a eye-catching diving save.

Tottenham have had more of the early possession, but both teams are still sounding each other out as we await the game’s first big chance. Palmers, Rogers and Henderson attempt a cheeky free kick routine, but Kinsky is alert to the danger.

Kinsky comes out of his box and Chelsea pounce on his poor pass to launch an attack. Palmer fizzes a delightful cross into the box, but no one is there to get on the end of it. Where’s Joao Pedro when you need him?

Rogers is playing highest for Chelsea as a false striker. He did it a few times for Villa, so it shouldn’t be anything new to him.

An early spell of Tottenham sees Chelsea defend a couple of free-kicks and clear a corner.

There will be no out-and-out strikers on the pitch today. Joao Pedro is out for Chelsea with an, as yet unspecified injury, while De Zerbi has said that Dominic Solanke “felt fatigue” against Coventry City so he has dropped to the bench. Antonio Conte, a former manager of both of these teams, wouldn’t be having a player missing a London derby for “feeling fatigue”.

Chelsea get us under way. The rain is hammering down on the pitch.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Chelsea and Tottenham at Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea secured a hard-fought 2-0 away win at Everton last weekend thanks to Pedro Neto’s double, while Tottenham earned their first Premier League victory of the season on Monday, beating Frank Lampard’s Coventry City 3-1 at home.

It’s Xabi Alonso’s first taste of the bitter rivalry and has hyped up the atmosphere ahead of the clash. “We are expecting a good atmosphere,” he said. “Electric, with good energy, knowing that in a derby this passion is really in the air in the stadium.

#1200. Report Milan have €70m Endrick offer ready for Real Madrid

Spanish reports claim Milan are ready to offer €70m in January for Real Madrid and Brazil striker Endrick, with Jose Mourinho the biggest obstacle to a sale.

Rossoneri patron Gerry Cardinale has made no secret of the fact he wants to bring in Endrick, repeatedly praising the youngster in the media.

Cadena SER suggest that the proposal is very much real, with €70m on the table for a January transfer.

Considering the lack of playing time he is getting at Real Madrid, the club is more than open to the potential exit, having invested €47.5m in buying him from Palmeiras in the summer of 2024.

However, Mourinho is adamant it would be a mistake to sell the 20-year-old so soon into his career, fearing he can flourish elsewhere.

We already saw glimpses of his capabilities during the loan experience at Olympique Lyonnais, but the report in Spain suggests Endrick is not prepared to take on another short-term move.

He wants some certainty in his career, and that means Milan could be the favourites.

It could ultimately come down to what Mourinho can promise, and whether Endrick believes it will be enough.

#1199. Leeds Need to Tie Farke Down After Tanaka and Calvert-Lewin Agreements

Leeds United are closing in on two important agreements as they look to progress in their second season back in the Premier League.

GIVEMESPORT exclusively revealed on Tuesday evening that Dominic Calvert-Lewin is close to signing a new deal to stay at Elland Road, having been a huge Leeds success following his free transfer move from Everton in the summer of 2025.

The 29-year-old has cemented his spot in Thomas Tuchel's England squad in recent months, and he has come off of the substitutes' bench in three of the Three Lions' previous six fixtures, including the famous win in Spain during the last international break.

Calvert-Lewin has been in fine goalscoring form for the Whites, which has led to interest from rivals Manchester United, as previously revealed by GMS sources.

The Red Devils are looking to sign a new centre-forward to compete with Benjamin Sesko following injury issues for the Slovenia international this term, but they won't be getting the Englishman with talks advanced over a new deal.

Meanwhile, Leeds are also in advanced discussions over extending the contract of Japan international Ao Tanaka, who has become one of their most important players following their return to England's top flight.

While the front two of Calvert-Lewin and Noah Okafor were brilliant in Saturday's 4-1 win against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge, Tanaka ran the show in midfield behind them and is fully deserving of a new deal in Yorkshire.

Tying the duo down is a big boost as Leeds look to secure a top-half finish this term, having comfortably escaped a relegation battle in the final weeks of last season.

Next, they need to finalise an even more important agreement with manager Daniel Farke.

Farke has sometimes been a bit of a divisive manager for the Elland Road faithful, especially after losing the 2024 Championship playoff final, and at points last season following their promotion to the Premier League.

There would have been some supporters at times last season who would have believed that the German wouldn't remain in charge of them for the long-term in Yorkshire, but he has ultimately done an outstanding job this term.

The 49ers backed the 50-year-old with some big summer signings like James Trafford, Tarik Muharemovic and Harry Wilson, and they currently lie in seventh position in the table.

As we approach December, they have only been beaten twice in the league, and their highlight of the season so far came on Saturday when they thrashed Chelsea 4-1 at Stamford Bridge.

Only the reigning champions Arsenal have conceded fewer goals than Leeds, and while their goalscoring had been a concern prior to their thumping win against Xabi Alonso's side, that game will give them confidence in their scoring abilities.

With Farke's contract currently due to expire at the end of the season, he is continuing to show that he is capable of taking the team forward to even better things if he has the right backing.

The Athletic reported last month that an agreement in principle had been reached over a new deal, but there is still no sign of the confirmation.

There could be more signings and other contract extensions to come in 2027, but tying Farke down has to be the urgent priority for the 49ers now, to remove any uncertainty around Elland Road.

By SIMON JONES and TOM COLLOMOSSE, FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 14:08 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:18 EST, 25 November 2026

Leeds United are in advanced talks with Japan international Ao Tanaka over a new contract.

The 28-year-old midfielder is close to agreeing terms on a deal that will keep him at Elland Road until 2029 with his current contract due to expire in the summer of 2028.

Leeds have lost only 10 games out of the 66 Tanaka has started since joining the club from Fortuna Dusseldorf in 2024. He has had an impressive start to the current campaign, becoming a key figure in Daniel Farke's side, starting in nine of Leeds' 11 Premier League matches. They currently sit seventh in the table.

Leeds have already tied down Ethan Ampadu to a four-year deal while Joe Rodon, Jayden Bogle and Brenden Aaronson all signed new contracts during the summer transfer window.

Talks are also expected to progress over a new deal for Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who has been linked with a move to bitter rivals Manchester United as they look to bolster their striking department.

Discussing Tanaka's form ahead of their emphatic win over Chelsea at the weekend, Farke said: 'It was a big ask for him after spending many years on second-tier level in Germany or here in the Championship.

Ao Tanaka (left) is in advanced talks with Leeds United over signing a new contract until 2029

Leeds are also in talks with striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin over a new deal to stay at Elland Road

'Last season was his first year in the top league. I think he’d shown glimpses of his potential, but he needed to find a bit of consistency. I would agree that he is finding this during the season.

'It was not always a 10 out of 10 performance but I think it's important for a player, once you're mature, that on the weaker days you're still a six or a seven out of 10, and this is what he's doing.

'So perhaps even on the more challenging days, he's at least solid and plays first of all with good confidence, like he always does, but also with a seriousness to be consistent and to work for the team, also against the ball, strong in the duels.

#1197. Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2. Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools3,4,5,6. Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST (PseCAST) shows the highest activity in mammalian cells so far7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution8. However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation9. Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the PseCAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the PseCAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade–TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa PseCAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC–TnsB and TnsB–target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.

Transposons are pervasive DNA segments capable of mobilizing within and between genomes, thus serving as potent drivers of genome evolution and horizontal gene transfer10,11,12. CASTs have evolved repeatedly by exaptation of minimal, nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas systems to enable RNA-guided, site-specific DNA integration13,14,15. These systems operate through the concerted action of a CRISPR-based targeting module and a Tn7-like transposition machinery comprising the TnsC AAA+ ATPase, the TnsB transposase and, in some systems, the TnsA endonuclease. The CASTs characterized so far differ mainly in the organization of their DNA-targeting and transposition modules1,2,16,17,18. Type I variants typically use a multi-subunit Cascade–TniQ (QCascade) complex for target recognition guided by CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and TnsA–TnsB for cut-and-paste transposition19,20,21. By contrast, type V-K systems rely on the Cas12k–TniQ–S15 complex for crRNA-guided targeting5 and use only TnsB for copy-and-paste transposition, resulting in cointegrate products22. TnsC plays a pivotal part in all CASTs, acting as an adapter that bridges the targeting module and the transposase enzymes to define the insertion site23,24.

The inherent programmability of CASTs has driven their development as genome-editing tools that enable the site-specific insertion of multi-kilobase DNA cargoes without generating double-stranded breaks in the target DNA. CAST-based editing has been implemented in bacteria25,26,27,28 and mammalian cells7,8,29,30, offering considerable potential for research and therapeutic applications. Type V-K CASTs generally show low integration efficiencies in human cell lines29,30, limited specificity2,26,27,31 and heterogeneous insertion profiles22,30. By contrast, type I-F systems can perform precise, simple insertions with substantially higher efficiencies1,7,22,26. In particular, the type I-F system of the Pseudoalteromonas Tn7016 transposon (Fig. 1a) has emerged as a highly promising candidate for genome-engineering applications, because of its uniquely high integration activity in human cells7,9. Directed evolution and structure-guided engineering of PseCAST components in Escherichia coli have resulted in the evoCAST system. This system has markedly improved integration efficiencies, reaching up to 10–30% in human cells, yet maintains precise, cointegrate-free insertion outcomes8. Although structural studies of type V-K CAST systems have provided mechanistic insights into various stages of transpososome assembly5,6,32,33,34,35,36, structural information about type I CASTs is currently limited to sub-complexes9,19,20,21,37,38,39,40,41,42. This presents a knowledge gap in the mechanistic understanding of the RNA-guided DNA-integration pathway. Specifically, the mechanism by which the RNA-guided targeting module induces the assembly and catalytic activation of the transposase components remains unclear.

a, Locus organization of the type I-F CAST of Pseudoalteromonas sp. S983 (Tn7016). RE, right transposon end; LE, left transposon end. b, Cryo-EM density map of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC targeting complex bound to DNA, coloured as in a. c, Atomic model of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC complex, coloured as in b. d, Schematic of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC complex, highlighting individual subunits. e, DNA organization in the targeting complex (left), with an accompanying diagram summarizing strand identity and protein footprints derived from the model (right). TGS, target strand; NTGS, non-target strand. f–h, Magnifications of the interactions between TniQ.1, TnsC.1 and TnsC.7, highlighting hydrophobic (f) and ionic (g) contacts as well as bridging interactions of TniQ.1 with the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 interface (h). i, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST containing mutations in the TniQ–TnsC interface, as determined by quantitative PCR (qPCR). j–l, Magnifications of the interaction interface between Cas8 and TnsC.5, highlighting electrostatic (j), polar (k) and aromatic (l) contacts. m, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST with mutations in the Cas8–TnsC interface, as determined by qPCR. i,m, Data are mean ± s.d. of three independent biological replicates (n = 3; circles); the catalytically inactive mutant TnsB(D220A) serves as a negative control.

Here we report a series of structural snapshots of the PseCAST system obtained using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), including a previously unresolved transpososome holocomplex assembly comprising all molecular components. These snapshots reveal the molecular determinants and critical checkpoints at key stages of the RNA-guided DNA-integration pathway, including target DNA recognition, TnsC oligomerization, transposase recruitment and catalytic activation. Our findings define the molecular mechanisms that govern RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs, thereby establishing a structural foundation for the further development of these systems as genome-engineering tools.

TnsC oligomers function as bridging modules for the assembly of the transposition machinery in both type V-K and type I-B CASTs, interacting with the RNA-guided CRISPR module through their amino-terminal face and with the transposase through their carboxy-terminal face6,20,36,41. To elucidate the structural basis of the guide-RNA-dependent assembly of TnsC in the type I-F PseCAST, our initial cryo-EM analysis yielded a reconstruction of a target-DNA-bound complex comprising PseCascade–TniQ and a heptameric TnsC ring (hereafter the targeting complex) at an overall resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 1b–d, Extended Data Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Resembling the architecture of TnsC heptamers from the canonical Tn7 element of E. coli and other type I CAST systems20,40,42,43 (Extended Data Fig. 2), the TnsC heptamer has a near-perfect seven-fold symmetry without a helical rise or seam, fully enclosing the DNA duplex in a positively charged central channel, in which all seven TnsC ATPase sites are occupied by ATP molecules and Mg2+ ions. The enclosed DNA adopts B-form geometry and is contacted by the Glu105–Asp120 loops of TnsC.1 and TnsC.5 through nonspecific interactions.

Notably, the structure of the targeting complex includes a complete 32-base-pair R-loop (Fig. 1e), which was only partially formed in the previously reported intermediate PseQCascade complex structure9. In contrast to the open arrangement of the partial R-loop intermediate9, the Cas8 α-helical bundle (residues 272–421) undergoes an approximately 90° rotation into a closed or locked state (Extended Data Fig. 3a), establishing additional contacts with the protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM)-distal segment of the target DNA, both TniQ subunits and Cas7.5 (Extended Data Fig. 3b–d). Moreover, three nucleotides of the displaced non-target strand (NTGS) are bound in a pocket in the Cas8 bundle (Extended Data Fig. 3e), which likely facilitates reannealing of the NTGS with the target strand (TGS) in the PAM-distal DNA segment and its interactions with the TniQ dimer. This feature is absent from the partial R-loop and open helical-bundle states of type I-F CAST QCascade complexes published previously19,21. As the presence of a full R-loop and a closed Cas8 helical-bundle conformation have been suggested to be a prerequisite for stable target engagement21, our structural observations indicate that the formation of the locked state serves as a target fidelity checkpoint upstream of transposase recruitment.

Unexpectedly, the structure of the PseCAST targeting complex revealed that the TnsC heptamer interacts with both TniQ.1 and Cas8 through extensive interfaces spanning 947 Å2 and 818 Å2, respectively (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 3f), forming a ‘super-ring’ assembly that bridges the PAM-proximal and PAM-distal ends of the QCascade subcomplex. At the N-terminal face of the heptamer, TnsC protomers use the same surfaces for interactions with both TniQ and Cas8 (Extended Data Fig. 3f). At the PAM-distal end, the N-terminal region of TniQ.1 is wedged into the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 inter-subunit interface. An aromatic pocket in TniQ.1 comprising Phe3, Phe5, Phe29 and Phe30 interacts with a hydrophobic loop in TnsC.1 containing Leu101, Leu104, Leu106, Phe107 and Ile112 (Fig. 1f). TnsC.1 further engages TniQ.1 in a series of ionic interactions (Fig. 1g) and bridging interactions that also contact the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 interface (Fig. 1h). Individual mutations in the inserted TnsC loop (L106S or F107A) did not affect the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli. By contrast, a strong synergistic effect in the TnsC double mutant L106A, F107A led to a near-complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 1i). Whereas alanine substitutions in pairs of residues in the TniQ hydrophobic pocket (either F3A and F5A, or F29A and F30A) had a mild effect on transposition efficiency (Fig. 1i), charge-reversal substitutions at these positions (either F3E and F5E, or F29E and F30E) had a substantially stronger effect (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Deletion of the seven N-terminal TniQ residues resulted in the loss of transposition activity (Fig. 1i). Moreover, cross-subunit mutant combinations involving residues in the TnsC loop and the TniQ hydrophobic pocket, either TnsC(L106S) and TniQ(F3A, F5A), or TnsC(F107A) and TniQ(F29A, F30A), resulted in a marked decrease in or the complete loss of transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 1i), confirming the importance of the TniQ–TnsC interactions for the assembly of the PseCAST transpososome.

At the PAM-proximal end, Cas8 and TnsC.5 form a shape-complementary interface, mediated by aromatic and electrostatic interactions (Fig. 1j–l). The combination of TnsC mutations R68A, Y75A, R77A and Pheresulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 1m), indicating that the Cas8–TnsC interaction contributes to transpososome assembly. However, mutations of interacting residues in Cas8, alone or in cross-subunit combinations with TnsC, had a mild or negligible effect (Fig. 1m), suggesting that the sensitivity of the TnsC–Cas8 interface to mutational perturbations is lower than that of the TnsC–TniQ interface. Similarly, whereas the individual charge-reversal TnsC mutant Y75E alone was sufficient to decrease transposition activity substantially, single charge-reversal mutations in Cas8 (T486R, W465E or H469E) had variable effects on transposition efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Together, these structural observations define the molecular coupling between the CRISPR targeting machinery and TnsC that results in the assembly of an ATP-loaded TnsC heptamer on the target DNA.

In the canonical Tn7 element in E. coli44, as well as in the type V-K CAST system of Scytonema hofmanni (ShCAST) and the type I-B CAST system of Peltigera membranacea cyanobiont 210A (PmcCAST), transposase recruitment is mediated by TnsC interactions with the C-terminal region of TnsB6,23,41. In the structure of the paired-end complex (PEC) of PseTnsAB, the C-terminal tail of PseTnsB (residues 574–613) is disordered45. To assess whether the unstructured tail plays a similar part in interacting with PseTnsC, we performed co-precipitation experiments using affinity-tagged PseTnsB constructs comprising either the full-length protein or the standalone C-terminal tail (TnsB(575–613)) (Fig. 2a). Both full-length TnsB and TnsB(575–613) co-precipitated target-DNA-bound QCascade and TnsC efficiently in the presence of ATP (Fig. 2b), indicating that TnsB interacts directly with the targeting complex and that its C-terminal tail is sufficient for this interaction. The amount of co-precipitated TnsC remained unchanged in the presence of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue ATPγS (Extended Data Fig. 4a), indicating that, similar to the type I-B PmcCAST system41,42, TnsB does not stimulate ATPase-dependent depolymerization of TnsC in PseCAST. Furthermore, co-precipitation of TnsC by TnsB(575–613) decreased strongly in the absence of ATP, suggesting that the interaction requires ATP-dependent TnsC oligomerization (Extended Data Fig. 4b). This result was corroborated by the loss of TnsC co-precipitation in the absence of QCascade or after introducing mutations in the TniQ- and Cas8-interacting interfaces (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Together, these results indicate that TnsB recruitment requires QCascade-dependent assembly of TnsC on the target DNA.

To validate these findings structurally, we aimed to reconstitute and determine the structure of QCascade–TnsC in complex with TnsAB bound to the excised transposon ends. To this end, we performed affinity co-precipitation using a recombinant TnsAB fusion protein construct (Fig. 2a), pre-assembled with a segment of the right end of the transposon (RE), to capture the QCascade–TnsC complex assembled on the target substrate comprising a linear double-stranded DNA (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Single-particle cryo-EM analysis of the resulting sample yielded a 2.8-Å reconstruction of a PseCAST transposase recruitment complex comprising target-bound QCascade and heptamerized TnsC decorated with TnsB C-terminal segments (or TnsB hooks; residues Trp605–Glu613). The TnsB hooks are bound to all TnsC subunits at the junction between the N-terminal α/β core domain and the C-terminal α-helical bundle close to the ATP binding pocket (Fig. 2c,d, Extended Data Table 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5a–c), similar to the arrangement described for type V-K34,36 and I-B41,42 CASTs (Extended Data Fig. 6). They are anchored by hydrophobic interactions of TnsB residues Trp605, Leu609 and Phe612 and an additional hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of residue Asp606 of TnsB and Arg212 of TnsC (Fig. 2e). Corroborating these observations, TnsB mutation W605A caused a substantial decrease in the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli. Moreover, individual TnsB mutations L609K or F612A, as well as the deletion of the entire TnsB hook (Δ604–613) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 2f). These findings highlight the functional requirement of the interactions between the TnsB hook and TnsC for the transposition activity of PseCAST and demonstrate the critical role of the TnsB C-terminal tail in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase and for the delivery of the transposon DNA to the target site before integration.

To determine the structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex comprising Cascade, TniQ, TnsC and TnsAB, we used a modified ‘one pot’ affinity co-precipitation strategy to trap the transpososome in a post-integration strand-transfer complex (STC) state (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7), which has been used previously to visualize transpososome structures because of its stability6,34,36,41,46,47. The assembly used a minimal symmetrized RE donor sequence, which supports transposition in related systems48,49 and is sufficient for the formation of a paired-end PseTnsAB complex45. Cryo-EM analysis of the resulting sample, supported by three-dimensional variability analysis combined with heterogeneous and locally focused refinement, yielded a reconstruction with a global resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 3b, Extended Data Table 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). The reconstruction revealed that the transposase adopts an intertwined, pseudo-twofold arrangement with a TnsA2–TnsB4 stoichiometry to assemble on the structured DNA in an STC configuration (Fig. 3c,d). All seven TnsC subunits are bound to the C-terminal hook motifs of TnsAB (Fig. 3b,c); it is not possible to ascertain which of these are connected to the bound TnsAB or contributed by unbound TnsAB molecules in trans, as the connecting segments (residues 824–843) of TnsAB are unstructured. The target DNA exits from the central channel of the TnsC heptamer and extends towards the TnsAB tetramer assembled on the pseudo-palindromic target site duplication (TSD) region and the adjacent transposon end sequences (Fig. 3a). As in the structure of the TnsAB PEC45, each transposon end is occupied by two TnsB protomers: a proximal catalytic subunit (TnsB.1 or TnsB.2)—the catalytic domain of which engages the other transposon end in trans—and a distal structural subunit (TnsB.3 or TnsB.4) (Fig. 3c). Only two TnsA subunits (TnsA.1 and TnsA.2), bound to the catalytic TnsB protomers, are resolved in the structure. The corresponding interaction interfaces in the structural TnsB subunits are occupied by the bound RE DNA duplexes, precluding TnsA interactions.

a, Schematic of the strand-transfer DNA-product mimic used for complex reconstitution, as modelled in the structure, with protein footprints highlighted. TR, terminal repeat. b, Cryo-EM density composite map of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex. c, Atomic model of the holocomplex, with protein subunits coloured as in Fig. 2c; individual TnsAB subunits are depicted in shades of orange. d, Atomic model of the strand-transfer DNA product, with distinct regions highlighted in different colours. e, Magnification of the interactions between the β-barrel domain of TnsB.1 and the TnsC.1 and TnsC.7 subunits. f, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST containing mutations in the TnsC–TnsB β-barrel domain interface, as quantified by qPCR. TnsC(316–321 GSGSGS) denotes a TnsC variant in which residues 316–321 were replaced with a (Gly–Ser)3 linker. Data are mean ± s.d. of three biologically independent replicates (n = 3; circles); TnsB mutation D220A serves as a negative control. g, Overview of contacts between the β-barrel and C-terminal helical TnsB domains and the target DNA duplex.

The structure of the PseCAST holocomplex reveals the molecular interactions responsible for the TnsC-dependent recruitment of TnsAB to the target DNA to effect site-specific donor integration. The TnsB.1 subunit is tethered to the C-terminal face of the TnsC heptamer by its β-barrel domain (residues 434–500), positioned at the interface of the TnsC.1 and TnsC.7 subunits (Fig. 3e). TnsC.1 inserts its C-terminal loop—spanning residues 314–322 and including Leu318—into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Val472, Gln467 and Leu441 in the TnsB.1 β-barrel domain (Fig. 3e). In turn, Asn316 of TnsC, situated in the same loop in TnsC.7, interacts through hydrogen bonds with Arg443 and Asn444 in TnsB.1 (Fig. 3e). Aspartate substitutions of Leu318 in TnsC (L318D) or Val472 in TnsB (V472D) resulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 3f). The single TnsC mutation N316A or replacement of TnsC loop residues 316–321 with a (Gly–Ser)3 linker resulted in modestly impaired activity. By contrast, the single TnsB mutations R443E or N444D strongly reduced transposition activity (Fig. 3f), confirming that the formation of this interface is essential for PseCAST-mediated DNA transposition.

In addition to interactions with TnsC, the β-barrel domain of the catalytic TnsB.1 subunit also interacts with the backbone of the target DNA segment downstream of the TnsC heptamer, forming a network of hydrogen bonds and electrostatic contacts using Arg439, Thr440, Lys447 and Gln449 of TnsB (Fig. 3g). Furthermore, Lys520 and Arg524 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB also contact the target DNA backbone. Notably, this domain adopts a helical bundle fold that bridges the catalytic and β-barrel domains in the catalytic TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits. By contrast, the helical domain of the structural TnsB.3 and TnsB.4 subunits forms two stretched helices that are sandwiched between the catalytic domain and DNA-binding domain 2 of TnsAB.1 and TnsAB.2, contributing to intra-subunit contacts.

Together, these insights highlight the functional role of the TnsB β-barrel domain in transpososome assembly. The shape complementarity of the TnsC and TnsB β-barrel interaction surfaces, together with cooperative interactions with the target DNA, provide the structural basis for the molecular ruler mechanism that defines the integration site, enabling the transposon to be inserted at a fixed distance of 49 nucleotides from the crRNA-specified target site. Moreover, the synergistic contacts with two TnsC subunits and the target DNA underlie a checkpoint mechanism that senses target DNA-dependent TnsC oligomerization, thereby explaining the strictly sequential assembly of the transpososome observed in type I-F systems40.

The structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex captures the TnsAB STC tetramer in a post-integration state (Fig. 4a,b). As in the PEC structure45, the active sites of the TnsA.1 and TnsA.2 subunits interact with the 5′ termini of the transposon ends, adopting a catalytically competent, post-cleavage geometry in which the catalytic triad residues Glu34, Asp71 and Lys87 of TnsA coordinate the 5′-terminal phosphate group and a single Mg2+ ion (Fig. 4c). In contrast to the PEC structure, the catalytic sites of the TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits also assume an activated conformation in which a Mg2+ ion—coordinated by the catalytic triad residues Asp220, Asp304 and Glu340 of TnsB—interacts with the 3′-hydroxyl group of the terminal nucleotide (dG76 in the NTGS) of the target DNA and the phosphodiester group that links the TSD segment to the 3′-terminal nucleotide of the transposon end (Fig. 4d). Furthermore, the catalytic domain establishes contacts with RE and TSD nucleotides that are crucial for STC formation (Fig. 4d). Specifically, Asp225 of TnsB positions an additional Mg2+ ion such that it simultaneously coordinates the phosphate groups of dA(−82) and dG(−80), stabilizing a kink in the DNA backbone at the TSD–RE junction that enables STC formation. The backbone is additionally contacted by Thr222, Arg239 and Ser360 of TnsB (Fig. 4d). Consistent with these observations, alanine substitution of Asp225 (D225A) or a charge-reversal mutation of Arg239 of TnsB (R239E) resulted in a complete loss of PseCAST transposition activity in E. coli, whereas TnsB mutations T222A or S360A only reduced PseCAST activity (Fig. 4e).
